content: The evidence for this question directly overlaps with the evidence reviewed for the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, specifically Module 2: Systematic Screening for Tuberculosis Disease, published in 2021. As a result, this PICO question was not addressed by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) during their meeting in May-June 2021. PICO Question 1: TB Screening Approaches in Children Under 10 Years of Age 1. Which screening tools should be used to systematically screen for TB disease in children under 10 years of age accessing healthcare? In children under 10 years of age accessing healthcare in high TB prevalence settings, should systematic screening for pulmonary TB (PTB) using chest radiography (CXR) be employed against a composite reference standard? In children under 10 years of age accessing healthcare in high TB prevalence settings, should systematic screening for pulmonary TB using symptom screening be employed against a composite reference standard? PICO Question 2: TB Diagnostic Approaches in Children 1. In children under 10 years of age with presumptive pulmonary TB attending healthcare facilities, should integrated treatment-decision algorithms be used to diagnose pulmonary TB compared to a microbiological or composite reference standard? 2. In children under 10 years of age with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB seeking care at healthcare facilities, should Xpert Ultra in gastric aspirate or stool be used to diagnose pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance compared to a microbiological/composite reference standard? What is the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert Ultra in gastric aspirate and stool for pulmonary TB in children under 10 years of age compared to a microbiological and composite reference standard? What is the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert Ultra in gastric aspirate and stool for rifampicin resistance in children under 10 years of age compared to a microbiological and composite reference standard? PICO Question 3: Treatment Shortening in Children and Adolescents with Non-Severe Drug-Susceptible TB 1. In children and adolescents with non-severe TB, should a 4-month intervention regimen versus the standard 6-month regimen conforming to WHO guidelines be used? PICO Question 4: Treatment of Rifampicin-Resistant/Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) 1. In MDR/RR-TB patients under 6 years of age, should an all-oral treatment regimen containing bedaquiline versus other regimens conforming to WHO guidelines without bedaquiline be used? 2. In MDR/RR-TB patients under 3 years of age, should an all-oral treatment regimen containing delamanid versus other regimens conforming to WHO guidelines without delamanid be used? PICO Question 5: Treatment of Pediatric TB Meningitis 1. In children and adolescents with presumed or bacteriologically confirmed drug-susceptible TB meningitis, should a 6-month intensive regimen compared to the 12-month regimen conforming to current WHO guidelines be used? PICO Question 6: Models of Care for TB Case Detection and TB Prevention 1. In children and adolescents with signs and symptoms of TB, should decentralization of child and adolescent TB services versus centralized child and adolescent TB services (at referral or tertiary hospital level) be used? 2. In children and adolescents exposed to TB, should decentralization of child and adolescent TB prevention and care services versus centralized prevention and care services (at referral or tertiary hospital level) be used to increase coverage of TB preventive treatment (TPT) in eligible children and adolescents? 3. In children and adolescents with signs and symptoms of TB, should family-centered, integrated services versus standard, non-family-centered, non-integrated services be used? 4. In children and adolescents exposed to TB, should family-centered, integrated services versus standard, non-family-centered, non-integrated services be used to increase coverage of TPT in eligible children and adolescents? Background Questions 1. What is the socioeconomic impact of TB on children and adolescents and their families? 2. How can adolescents with TB or eligible for TPT be optimally engaged in their care? Publication, Dissemination, Evaluation, and Expiry The electronic version of the consolidated guidelines on the management of TB in children and adolescents will be part of the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform (KSP). This platform includes consolidated guidelines, operational handbooks with implementation guidance, and a catalog of WHO e-learning materials. Dissemination strategies include global, regional, and country webinars and consultations, development of training materials based on the guidelines and operational handbook, and technical support for countries during program reviews and other in-country missions. Data collected for the annual global TB reports will be evaluated to monitor TB notification rates for children (0–4 and 5–9 years) and adolescents (10–14 and 15–19 years), the proportion of notified TB cases that are children and young adolescents under 15 years (for both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB), and TB treatment coverage rates for children under 5 years, children, and young adolescents aged 5–14 years. Other indicators include TB treatment outcomes for children and young adolescents under 15 years and coverage of TPT among eligible contacts under 5 years and older contacts. Recommendations in the 2022 consolidated guidelines will be considered for updating in five years or earlier if new evidence becomes available. For the interim recommendation on the use of treatment decision algorithms, new data will be generated and reviewed within a two-year period. Document Structure 1. Chapter 1: Introduction, background information, scope (including PICO and background questions), rationale, objectives, and target audience for the guidelines. 2. Chapter 2: WHO recommendations on TB screening and contact investigation relevant to children and adolescents. This includes systematic screening for TB disease and contact investigation, with recommendations on populations to be screened and screening tools to be applied. 3. Chapter 3: TB prevention, including recommendations on TB infection prevention and control, TPT, and BCG vaccination. 4. Chapter 4: Diagnostic approaches, including new recommendations on the use of Xpert Ultra in gastric aspirate and stool specimens and integrated treatment decision algorithms for children with presumptive pulmonary TB. 5. Chapter 5: TB treatment, including new recommendations on a 4-month regimen for non-severe drug-susceptible TB, a 6-month intensive regimen for TB meningitis, and the use of bedaquiline and delamanid for MDR/RR-TB. 6. Chapter 6: Models of care, including new recommendations on decentralized care and integrated family-centered care. 7. Chapter 7: Specific situations such as care for children and adolescents with TB and HIV, TB and malnutrition, and feeding of infants born to mothers with TB. 8. Chapter 8: Research priorities identified at the 2021 GDG meeting, highlighting areas where additional evidence is needed to improve TB prevention, management, and care in children and adolescents.
